extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in philosophy of science, logic, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing inductive inferences, analogical arguments, and the extension of empirical and causal laws across time and place; plus standards for what counts as evidence for universal causation. Focused on when analogies or inductions are strong enough to justify belief or further inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative laws contingent on collocations
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative uniformities (those of co-existence and sequence derived from more ultimate laws) are contingent on the collocation of primeval causes; if collocations vary, different derivative uniformities may result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These derivative uniformities are admissible only where the collocations are known by experience to be such as are requisite for the truth of the law; that is, only within the conditions of time and place confirmed by actual observation. They are therefore more infirm and more contingent than ultimate causal laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of derivative laws limited to adjacent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A derivative (non-causative) law can be extended beyond observed cases only to adjacent cases in time or circumstance; further extension weakens the induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: confidence that the sun will rise 'to-morrow' is warranted, but extending the same induction many thousands of years into the future becomes progressively less reliable. The farther into the future (or remote cases) one projects, the weaker the inductive warrant becomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of causes strengthens and extends induction
rubrics_metrics.description: When the causes on which a uniformity depends are known, one can extend the derivative uniformity farther in time and place and with greater assurance than when only an empirical law is known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing the causes allows judgment about known potential counteracting causes and about the extreme boundaries of the causes' influence; this both enlarges spatial extent of safe extrapolation and reduces uncertainty about counteraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical laws extended across space only under shared influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws can be extended to other places only when those places are presumably within the influence of the same individual agents or identical origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If effects can be traced to an identical (not merely similar) origin, we may extend the empirical law to all places within the extreme local boundaries of the ascertained influence of those causes, subject to the possibility of counteracting causes in parts of the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy as resemblance of relations (fundamentum relationis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy, understood as resemblance of relations, can be as conclusive as induction if the circumstance in which two cases resemble (the fundamentum relationis) is the material circumstance on which consequences depend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the common relation is shown to be the determining material circumstance (e.g., management by a few persons), an analogical inference may amount to a rigorous induction; otherwise the analogy fails to be conclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between analogy and induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogical reasoning (two things resemble in some respects; a proposition true of one, therefore probably true of the other) differs from complete induction because it lacks demonstration of an invariable conjunction between shared properties and the inferred property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat analogy as induction unless a prior comparison of instances has established an invariable link (via Methods of Agreement/Difference). Analogy supplies probability, not certainty, unless such a conjunction is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require that shared properties are not known to be irrelevant
rubrics_metrics.description: For an analogical argument to be admissible, the properties common to A and B must not be known to be unconnected with the inferred attribute m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any common properties can be shown (by elimination or prior laws) to be immaterial to m, the analogy is invalidated. The presumption must be that m depends on some property of A which is among the undetermined ones that B also possesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight ultimate-property resemblance over derivative-property resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: Resemblance in ultimate (fundamental) properties confers greater strength to an analogical inference than resemblance in derivative properties; likeness in ultimate properties can make derivative resemblances nearly certain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If B resembles A in ultimate properties, expect resemblance in many derivative properties. If resemblance is only in derivative properties, there is reason to suspect (but not be sure of) resemblance in ultimate properties and further derivates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known dissimilarities produce counter-probabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Every proved dissimilarity between A and B furnishes a counter-probability against the analogical inference comparable in nature to the probability arising from resemblances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the competition between known agreements and known differences; as known differences grow, they can outweigh resemblances. Unknown properties' vastness reduces weight of partial resemblances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicting analogies reduce inferential power
rubrics_metrics.description: When a new case resembles cases where the property m exists and also resembles cases where m does not exist, the analogical evidence is conflicted and weakened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include objects resembling works of multiple artists or substances sharing properties with different classes; unless one set of resemblances can be shown material, analogical inference is unsettled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy valuable as a heuristic, not a final proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy, even when weak as proof, is highly valuable in suggesting experiments or observations that may lead to conclusive inductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogical hypotheses to 'bring new ones to light' and to design experimenta crucis; do not accept hypotheses as scientific truths merely because they are plausible analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogical strength depends on adjacency in circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogical inferences are most valuable when the new case is 'adjacent' to known cases in circumstances (not merely time/place but relevant conditions); adjacency increases probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A new case sharing most of the numerous conditions known to accompany an effect (with only a few missing) can yield a high-probability analogical inference; nevertheless seek complete induction when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative heuristic: proportion of known agreement approximates probability
rubrics_metrics.description: When B agrees with A in most known properties, the probability that B has a given derivative property of A increases roughly in proportion to the degree of agreement (e.g., nine of ten known properties gives about 9:1 odds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a heuristic, not a formal rule; it indicates that extensive observed resemblance can make analogical inference approach the strength of induction, but unknown properties may still dominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive methods presuppose universality of causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods such as Agreement and Difference assume that every event has some cause; the validity of these inductive methods depends on the universality of causation being true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that inference from instances using these methods implicitly takes for granted that effects must have assignable antecedents; this assumption requires justification rather than blind acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief or instinct is not evidence for universal causation
rubrics_metrics.description: The universality of causation cannot be justified simply by the fact that people instinctively believe it; belief is not proof and does not dispense with the necessity of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence should be that which the judging faculty ought to yield to—sense and consciousness and conformity to fact—not mere psychological disposition. Do not accept a proposition as true merely because it is universally believed.
